steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for an information retrieval paper on aligning LLMs, without supervision, so their responses capture what makes each document distinct from similar ones. Explain the gap in existing alignment methods, introduce our contrastive-feedback framework, and summarize the experiments and contributions.

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown promising performance in a wide range of research fields, and information retrieval (IR) is one of them. IR aims to fulfil the information needs of individuals by locating relevant documents from a large-scale corpus, and it plays a fundamental role in the digital era. Previous studies have used LLMs in IR tasks like generating search snippets, doing query or document expansion, creating training data for retrieval models, and so on. These studies show that LLMs have significant potential in IR.

However, even though they are widely adopted, using an off-the-shelf LLM directly for IR tasks could be suboptimal. One key reason is that the capabilities of off-the-shelf LLMs are misaligned with the needs of IR tasks, especially the capability to give responses that capture what is distinctive about each document among similar documents. For example, Figure 1 shows the results of FLAN-T5 when used for document summarization, a representative IR task. We can see that off-the-shelf FLAN-T5 generates the same summary for three different documents, so a human cannot tell them apart. Such summaries are not acceptable as document representations or search snippets in search engines, because they do not help users find the documents they want quickly and accurately.

One of the most widely used methods to give LLMs the response attributes we want is LLM alignment. The idea of LLM alignment is to build feedback on the LLM's responses based on preferred attributes (e.g., helpfulness, harmlessness, etc.) and use it to optimize the LLM. Depending on how the feedback is collected, existing LLM alignment methods can be roughly divided into human-based methods and model-based methods. Unfortunately, none of the existing alignment methods can be used to improve the distinctiveness of LLM responses.

- Human-based methods such as RLHF are flexible and generic, but collecting large-scale human feedback is expensive and usually prohibitive in IR scenarios.

- Existing model-based methods such as RLAIF and RLCD do not need a human in the loop, but they cannot capture distinctiveness by design, because their feedback signals (i.e., reward scores) are computed point-wise. The distinctive information of an LLM response has to be specified in the context of other similar responses, so feedback signals of distinctiveness can only come from differentiating multiple responses group-wise, which existing methods clearly cannot do.

- RLCF
  - Reinforcement Learning from Contrastive Feedback, group-wise and fully unsupervised (Figure 2)
  - find group of similar documents per document; feed each to the LLM (e.g. summaries)
  - contrastive feedback with group-wise reciprocal rank reward; optimize with PPO
- Experiments
  - document summarization, document expansion, data augmentation
  - 770M to 11B; encoder-decoder and decoder-only; Chinese and English corpora
  - summarization: human evaluation, Rouge-diff; expansion/augmentation: downstream retrieval
  - RLCF significantly improves distinctiveness, benefits IR applications
- Contributions
  - first study of distinctiveness of LLM responses for IR
  - RLCF, contrastive feedback for unsupervised alignment with IR needs
  - effective for English and Chinese LLMs, scales and architectures

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown promising performance in a wide range of research fields, and information retrieval (IR) is one of them. IR aims to fulfil the information needs of individuals by locating relevant documents from a large-scale corpus, and it plays a fundamental role in the digital era. Previous studies have used LLMs in IR tasks like generating search snippets, doing query or document expansion, creating training data for retrieval models, and so on. These studies show that LLMs have significant potential in IR.

However, even though they are widely adopted, using an off-the-shelf LLM directly for IR tasks could be suboptimal. One key reason is that the capabilities of off-the-shelf LLMs are misaligned with the needs of IR tasks, especially the capability to give responses that capture what is distinctive about each document among similar documents. For example, Figure 1 shows the results of FLAN-T5 when used for document summarization, a representative IR task. We can see that off-the-shelf FLAN-T5 generates the same summary for three different documents, so a human cannot tell them apart. Such summaries are not acceptable as document representations or search snippets in search engines, because they do not help users find the documents they want quickly and accurately.

One of the most widely used methods to give LLMs the response attributes we want is LLM alignment. The idea of LLM alignment is to build feedback on the LLM's responses based on preferred attributes (e.g., helpfulness, harmlessness, etc.) and use it to optimize the LLM. Depending on how the feedback is collected, existing LLM alignment methods can be roughly divided into human-based methods and model-based methods. Unfortunately, none of the existing alignment methods can be used to improve the distinctiveness of LLM responses.

- Human-based methods such as RLHF are flexible and generic, but collecting large-scale human feedback is expensive and usually prohibitive in IR scenarios.

- Existing model-based methods such as RLAIF and RLCD do not need a human in the loop, but they cannot capture distinctiveness by design, because their feedback signals (i.e., reward scores) are computed point-wise. The distinctive information of an LLM response has to be specified in the context of other similar responses, so feedback signals of distinctiveness can only come from differentiating multiple responses group-wise, which existing methods clearly cannot do.

To address these limitations and improve the distinctiveness of LLM responses, we propose a new optimization framework called Reinforcement Learning from Contrastive Feedback (RLCF). RLCF is a group-wise alignment method that builds feedback of distinctiveness for a group of similar inputs, and it is fully unsupervised. Figure 2 shows the workflow of RLCF. First we find a group of similar documents for each document in the corpus. Then each document in the group is given to an LLM to get a response. For example, the responses could be summaries of long documents for a summarization task. Next we build contrastive feedback from the group of LLM-generated responses with a reward function called group-wise reciprocal rank. Finally, the LLM is optimized on the contrastive feedback with the standard Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) algorithm.

To show that RLCF is effective in optimizing the distinctiveness of LLM responses, we run comprehensive experiments with three representative IR tasks, LLMs of different scales (from 770M to 11B) with both encoder-decoder and decoder-only architectures, and both Chinese and English corpora. Specifically, we evaluate RLCF on document summarization, document expansion and data augmentation. The performance on these tasks is basically sensitive to the distinctiveness of the LLM-generated responses (e.g., summaries). For document summarization we evaluate the quality of the LLM-generated summaries directly, with human evaluation and an automatic metric called Rouge-diff. For document expansion and data augmentation, we evaluate the LLM responses through downstream document retrieval tasks, i.e., we compare the performance of retrieval models enhanced by LLMs with different alignment methods. The results show that compared to existing alignment methods, RLCF can significantly improve the distinctiveness of LLM responses, and this can largely benefit various IR applications.

Our main contributions are:

- As far as we know, we are the first to study the distinctiveness of LLM responses and show its significance for powering IR applications.

- We propose a new framework, RLCF, which uses contrastive feedback to align the capability of LLMs with the needs of IR without supervision.

- The experimental results show that RLCF is effective on both English and Chinese LLMs and on different parameter scales and architectures.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated promising performance across a wide range of research fields, including information retrieval (IR). IR aims to fulfil the information needs of individuals by locating relevant documents from a large-scale corpus [1], and plays a fundamental role in the digital era [2,3,4]. Previous studies have utilized LLMs in IR tasks such as generating search snippets [5,6,7,8], conducting query or document expansion [9,10,11], and creating training data for retrieval models [12,13,14]. These studies have demonstrated the significant potential of LLMs in IR.

However, while widely adopted, directly applying an off-the-shelf LLM to IR tasks could be suboptimal. One key reason is the misalignment between the capabilities of off-the-shelf LLMs and the needs of IR tasks, particularly the capability to provide responses that capture the distinctiveness of each document among similar documents [14,9]. For instance, Figure 1 shows the results of FLAN-T5 [15] when used for document summarization, a representative IR task. As we can see, off-the-shelf FLAN-T5 generates the same summary for three different documents, making them indistinguishable to humans. Such summaries are not acceptable as document representations or search snippets in search engines, as they fail to help users quickly and accurately locate the documents they want.

To empower LLMs with desired response attributes, one of the most widely adopted methods is LLM alignment. The idea of LLM alignment is to construct feedback on the LLM's responses based on preferred attributes (e.g., helpfulness [16], harmlessness [17,18,19], etc.) and use it to optimize the LLM. Depending on how the feedback is collected, existing LLM alignment methods can be broadly categorized into human-based and model-based methods. Unfortunately, none of the existing alignment methods can be used to improve the distinctiveness of LLM responses.

- While human-based methods such as RLHF [16] are flexible and generic, collecting large-scale human feedback is expensive and usually prohibitive in IR scenarios.

- While existing model-based methods such as RLAIF [17] and RLCD [18] do not require a human in the loop, they are inherently incapable of capturing distinctiveness, as their feedback signals (i.e., reward scores) are computed in a point-wise manner. The distinctive information of an LLM response must be specified in the context of other similar responses, so feedback signals of distinctiveness can only be derived by differentiating multiple responses in a group-wise manner, which existing methods clearly cannot do.

To address these limitations and improve the distinctiveness of LLM responses, we propose a novel optimization framework called Reinforcement Learning from Contrastive Feedback (RLCF). RLCF is a group-wise alignment method that constructs feedback of distinctiveness for a group of similar inputs, and it is fully unsupervised. The workflow of RLCF is depicted in Figure 2. Specifically, we first identify a group of similar documents for each document in the corpus. Then, each document in the group is fed to an LLM to obtain a corresponding response; for example, the responses could be summaries of long documents for a summarization task. Next, we construct contrastive feedback from the group of LLM-generated responses using a reward function named group-wise reciprocal rank. Finally, the LLM is optimized on the contrastive feedback with the standard Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) algorithm [20].

To demonstrate the effectiveness of RLCF in optimizing the distinctiveness of LLM responses, we conduct comprehensive experiments covering three representative IR tasks, various scales of LLMs (ranging from 770M to 11B) with both encoder-decoder and decoder-only architectures, and both Chinese and English corpora. In particular, we evaluate RLCF on document summarization, document expansion and data augmentation, tasks whose performance is essentially sensitive to the distinctiveness of the LLM-generated responses (e.g., summaries). For document summarization, we directly evaluate the quality of the LLM-generated summaries through human evaluation and an automatic metric called Rouge-diff. For document expansion and data augmentation, we evaluate the LLM responses through downstream document retrieval tasks, i.e., by comparing the performance of retrieval models enhanced by LLMs with different alignment methods. The results indicate that, compared to existing alignment methods, RLCF can significantly improve the distinctiveness of LLM responses, which can largely benefit various IR applications.

We summarize our main contributions as follows:

- To the best of our knowledge, we are the first to study the distinctiveness of LLM responses and demonstrate its significance in powering IR applications.

- We propose a novel framework, RLCF, which uses contrastive feedback to align the capability of LLMs with the needs of IR in an unsupervised way.

- The experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of RLCF on both English and Chinese LLMs, as well as on various parameter scales and architectures.
